In the line graph each of those edges becomes a node of the same color, named after it, and two nodes are joined when their edges share an endpoint; AB and CD share none, so they stay unconnected." width="100%"} The line graph `L(G)` of a graph `G` transforms edges into nodes: each edge in `G` becomes a node in `L(G)`, and two nodes in `L(G)` are connected if and only if their corresponding edges in `G` share an endpoint. Turning edges into nodes lets you apply any node-level tool to edges. Common uses: - finding edge communities (overlapping communities of nodes) by running a community detection method on the line graph - computing centrality of edges, e.g., which road segments or links are most central - modeling transfers in transport networks, where moving from one route segment to the next happens at a shared stop - edge coloring problems, which become node coloring problems on `L(G)` For an undirected graph, every pair of edges meeting at a node is connected, so a node of degree `d` contributes `d * (d - 1) / 2` edges to the line graph. Line graphs of graphs with hubs can therefore be much larger than the original. For a directed graph, edge `(u, v)` is linked to edge `(v, w)` only when the first edge ends where the second begins, which follows paths through the network. Each line-graph node is labelled `"-"` using the original node *IDs* (e.g., `"1-2"`). If the graph has parallel edges between the same pair of nodes, the original edge ID is appended (e.g., `"1-2-e3"`) to keep labels unique. Original node attributes are not carried over, and line-graph edges have no weights or attributes. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [create_using_directed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether the resulting line graph should be marked as directed. - If `None` (default): inherits directedness from source graph - If `True`: creates a directed line graph - If `False`: creates an undirected line graph This only sets the directedness of the returned graph; which pairs of edges are connected is always decided by the directedness of the *source* graph. For a directed source, edge `(u,v)` connects to edge `(v,w)` if they share the intermediate node `v` (i.e., head of first = tail of second); with `create_using_directed=False` those same connections are kept but without direction. For an undirected source with `create_using_directed=True`, each connection becomes a single directed edge from the lower to the higher line-graph node ID, not a pair. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new Graph representing the line graph. Each node in the line graph corresponds to an edge in the original graph, with attributes: - `original_edge_id`: ID of the original edge - `original_source`: node ID of the original edge's source - `original_target`: node ID of the original edge's target - `original_weight`: weight of the original edge (only present if it has one) A graph with no edges gives an empty line graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For a graph $G = (V, E)$, the line graph $L(G)$ has one node for each edge of $G$, with two nodes in $L(G)$ adjacent whenever the corresponding edges of $G$ share an endpoint. On directed graphs the sharing must respect direction: edge $(u, v)$ links to $(v, w)$ but not to $(w, v)$. From that definition follow several handy identities. $|V(L(G))| = |E(G)|$ by construction, and for undirected $G$ the edge count is $|E(L(G))| = \tfrac{1}{2} \sum_v \deg(v)^2 - |E(G)|$. The line graph of $K_n$ is the triangular graph $T(n)$; the line graph of an $n$-cycle is another $n$-cycle; and the line graph of a star $K_{1,n}$ is the complete graph $K_n$, because all $n$ spokes share the hub. Whitney's theorem (1932) makes the whole construction robust: except for the degenerate case of $K_3$ vs $K_{1,3}$, $L(G) \cong L(H)$ implies $G \cong H$. That property is what makes line graphs useful for edge clustering, edge-community analysis, and modeling transfer points in transportation networks. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~edge_coloring`) : Color edges directly. [](`~greedy_color`) : Color nodes, such as the nodes of a line graph. [](`~is_valid_edge_coloring`) : Check that no two edges at a node share a color. [](`~clique_graph`) : The graph of which maximal cliques overlap. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The path "A -- B -- C" has two edges, so its line graph has two nodes. They are joined because both edges meet at "B": ::: {#abbfbcd3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec path = ec.Graph.from_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) lines = path.line_graph() lines.count_nodes(), lines.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (2, 1) ``` ::: ::: All four spokes of a star meet at the center, so every pair of them is joined and the line graph is the complete graph on four nodes, with 6 edges: ::: {#eaf926eb .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} star = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("C", "L1"), ("C", "L2"), ("C", "L3"), ("C", "L4")] ) star.line_graph().count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 6 ``` ::: ::: Each line-graph node records the edge it came from, so results on the line graph can be mapped back: ::: {#2c62e5a7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} weighted = ec.Graph.from_edges([("X", "Y", 2.0), ("Y", "Z", 3.0)]) weighted.line_graph().get_node_df().select( "label", "original_edge_id", "original_source", "original_target", "original_weight", ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Scheduling handover sessions Each edge of the teams network joins a worker to a task they're qualified for. Before the assignment is made, every worker spends an hour with each of those tasks' teams. A worker can only be in one session at a time, and each team can host only one, so two sessions clash when they share a worker or a task. Clashing sessions are edges that share an endpoint, which are exactly the nodes joined in the line graph. Giving sessions hours so that no two clash is coloring the edges of the network, and that's the same as coloring the nodes of its line graph: ::: {#50356b0d .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} teams = ec.teams() sessions = teams.line_graph() hours = sessions.greedy_color() len(set(hours.values())) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 4 ``` ::: ::: Four hours is the fewest possible, since Omar is qualified for four tasks and Testing has four qualified workers. Mapped back to the edges, the hours are a valid edge coloring: ::: {#b90080f9 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} origins = sessions.get_node_df().select("id", "original_edge_id") edge_of = dict(origins.iter_rows()) schedule = {edge_of[session]: hour for session, hour in hours.items()} teams.is_valid_edge_coloring(schedule) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Here each session is an edge colored by its hour, with the tasks along the top and the workers along the bottom. No worker or task has two edges of one color: ::: {#788db040 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} teams.set_edge_attrs("hour", schedule) teams.layout_bipartite(align="horizontal", aspect_ratio=0.25) teams.plot( layout="pos", label_by="label", edge_color_by="hour", edge_width=3, edge_opacity=1, height=300, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: In the line graph, each session is a node, colored the same way, and no two joined nodes share a color: ::: {#f3130686 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} name = teams.get_label_from_id sessions.set_node_attrs("hour", hours) sessions.set_node_attrs( "session", { session: f"{name(u)}: {name(v)}" for session, u, v in sessions.get_node_df() .select("id", "original_source", "original_target") .iter_rows() }, ) sessions.layout_kamada_kawai() sessions.plot(layout="pos", color_by="hour", label_by="session") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
